query: For steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to corrosion? Specify a controlled study capable of revealing the governing cause, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting evidence from prior findings, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In stainless steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, enhanced corrosion resistance arises from the rapid self-healing of a Cr2O3-rich passive film. This self-healing is enabled by a fine-grained microstructure with high grain boundary density that promotes Cr diffusion from the bulk to the surface, quickly replenishing any lost or damaged oxide at localized corrosion sites.
generation.material_initial_state: Conventional stainless steel with standard Cr content and a relatively coarse-grained microstructure typical for chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications.
generation.intervention: Apply controlled thermomechanical processing (e.g., rolling and appropriate annealing) to produce a fine-grained variant with increased grain boundary area while keeping the Cr content constant.
generation.conditions: Corrosion tests performed in simulated chemical-processing and nuclear reactor water environments at elevated temperatures (and, if feasible, under controlled irradiation or aggressive chemical conditions) that mimic service conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: A continuous, Cr-enriched, thin passive film (predominantly Cr2O3) whose formation and repair are enhanced by the higher density of grain boundaries in the refined microstructure.
generation.mechanism: The refined grain structure accelerates Cr diffusion along grain boundaries, allowing efficient repair of the passive oxide film when it is compromised. This dynamic re-passivation limits localized metal dissolution and retards further corrosion under harsh thermal and chemical conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the coarse-grained baseline, the fine-grained steel will form a more uniform and stable Cr2O3 passive film, exhibit lower corrosion current densities and mass loss rates, and show improved electrochemical impedance characteristics in accelerated corrosion tests.
generation.baseline: Standard, coarse-grained stainless steel with unmodified grain structure, which develops a passive film at a slower rate and exhibits higher corrosion rates under similar test conditions.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be operative under service temperatures and radiation levels typical of chemical-processing and nuclear environments, provided the Cr content remains sufficiently high. Its effectiveness may diminish if the passive film is excessively disrupted by extreme environmental conditions or if the alloy composition is altered (for example, by lower Cr levels or interference from detrimental secondary phases).
generation.uncertainty: The relative contributions of intrinsic alloy chemistry versus grain boundary density in re-passivation kinetics remain not fully quantified, and the impact of irradiation on grain boundary diffusion in-service is uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of otherwise identical stainless steel samples: one with a conventional (coarse-grained) microstructure and one processed to achieve a significantly finer grain size without altering Cr content. Expose both sets to accelerated corrosion environments simulating chemical-processing and nuclear conditions (e.g., high-temperature aqueous salt solution, possibly with controlled irradiation). Monitor the formation, stability, and repair of the passive film using electrochemical tests and surface analytical techniques.
measurements: Potentiodynamic polarization to determine corrosion current densities
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) to assess oxide film integrity
Surface analysis (XPS/EDS) to quantify Cr enrichment and passive film thickness
Mass loss measurements over an extended period
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the fine-grained steel does not exhibit a statistically significant lower corrosion rate, improved impedance characteristics, or more stable and Cr-rich passive film compared to the coarse-grained baseline under identical test conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Paper card. Question: How does the molten salt corrosion behavior of the dual-phase AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy compare to conventional duplex stainless steel 2205 in a NaCl-KCl-MgCl2 environment at temperatures relevant to concentrating solar power systems?. System: AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) and duplex stainless steel 2205 (DS2205). Processing: Vacuum-arc-melting of high purity constituent elements (99.95 wt.% purity) with multiple re-melts for homogeneity; samples cut to 20 mm × 5 mm × 2 mm, polished to 1200-grit, degreased with acetone, and dried; corrosion tests performed in a custom tube furnace with 20 mm salt melt depth at 450 °C and 650 °C for 24 h. Test conditions: Molten NaCl-KCl-MgCl2 salt (45.4 wt.% MgCl2, 33 wt.% NaCl, 21.6 wt.% KCl) at 450 °C and 650 °C; immersion for 24 h; electrochemical measurements including OCP (1 h stabilization) and potentiodynamic polarization (-0.5 to 1.5 V at 1 mV/s). Findings: Corrosion rate of AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 was ~1 mm/year at 450 °C compared to ~8 mm/year for DS2205.; Corrosion rate of AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 was ~9 mm/year at 650 °C compared to ~20 mm/year for DS2205.; Mass loss for DS2205 at 650 °C was ~69 m
